lf-ask.description: One complete request to the reader: the heading, context, evidence, and answer control they need to consider it as a unit. It wraps exactly one non-quoted widget whose entry declares x-awaits; that nested widget still owns the action and determines whether the request is open. Use this when the request begins before its actionable widget — most often a section's heading and introductory prose above an lf-options group — so the Asks tray names the whole region and `n`/`p` arrives at its opening rather than dropping the reader straight into the answers. Keep the ordinary semantic section around it when the surrounding document needs a section landmark. The wrapper adds no frame or caption of its own.
lf-ask.x-example:
What a full store does

The beta never reached the cap. This decides what the first workspace at it sees.

Drop the oldest documents Editing continues. Pause offline editing Nothing leaves.

lf-options.description: A question the reader answers, and the alternatives it is about. `label` is that question, written on the group: the runtime renders it as the group's own first words (x-says), so the question is part of what the group says rather than a heading standing beside it. That is what lets anything reading the page's open asks name this one — a list of them has only the ask's own words to go on, and a group that holds no part of its question reads as its first option's chip band. It is also what lets a reader quote the question the way they quote an answer. Write it wherever the group would have a heading over it, and drop that heading rather than keeping a second copy of the question beside the thing that asks it. When the premise or evidence begins above the group, wrap that broader reading and this one group in lf-ask; the group keeps owning the choice while navigation arrives at the wrapper's opening. Children are lf-option elements only, and the form follows what they hold: an option leading with a <strong> title is a full-width card, and the cards stack — read down the page like a decision record, whether an option's case is one sentence or paragraphs with a `<dl class="facts">` rail — so a decision with real argument keeps its comparison, its detail and its evidence inside the group rather than growing a table or an 'in detail' section beside it, and the group holds one shape at three options or six; a group whose options are bare labels renders as compact rows, for a question whose alternatives are sections of the page rather than cards (each row's `for` names one). Nothing declares which — write the options and the look follows. With `choose` (which requires an id), the reader picks — by click, or by keyboard via the toggle mark each option carries, which is also where its state reads. The group itself then draws as one control in every form, cells sharing hairlines rather than options standing apart — the question is the first of those cells, holding its words off the frame and opening at the column the options open at — and that shape is what says a decision is waiting: the mark says nothing until there is a pick to state, so no option captions itself with an offer. Clicking a picked option again clears it. `multiple` (which requires `choose`) makes the pick a set rather than one option, for "which of these" rather than "which one". The marks say which of the two it is, in the pair every reader already has: a round mark takes one, a square mark takes any, and under `multiple` an option not yet picked draws its empty box in every form, since an untaken slot is that option's own state rather than the group's offer repeated. A shape reaches no screen reader, so a mark says the same thing in words there, reading "choose one" or "choose any". Write the question and leave the arity to the marks; a page that spells out how many picks the control will take is captioning it. On the page a `choose` group owns an ordinary comment thread for words its options don't cover — "none of these", or a pick's why. Its conversation stays beside the question and in Comments; interactive reply markup renders only in Comments. In a thread (the group as a reply's or comment's markup — the AskUserQuestion shape) the thread's own reply box is already that channel, so the group adds no conversation; a `multiple` group there carries a Done press instead, whose `answer` action states the set is whole — every toggle reaches the agent as it lands, so the press is the one thing a live channel can't derive, and the ask stands until it (see until in $awaits). The keyboard answers a group wherever it stands: Tab reaches a mark, ↑/↓ walk the options, ⏎ toggles, and 1–9 pick the nth outright — each option wears its digit while a mark holds focus. The pick reaches the agent as a `choose` action naming every picked option, empty once cleared, and carries onto every later version by itself — marking the picked options `chosen` in the next version is how the record reads without the log, not what keeps the pick alive. A pick rests on the options picked, so rewriting what one of them says needs its `restated` (see $restated in `page catalog`); a pick the reader has cleared rests on the group, and takes the group's. `settled` (also requiring an id) retires a decision that has been made and acted on: the group collapses to one line naming the chosen option, with the question still above it and every option and its conversation behind a disclosure the reader can open — the record keeps its ids and its anchors, and stops spending the page's height. Mark it once the choice has stopped being live, which is usually a version or two after honoring the pick, not the moment it was made; a settled group still takes a pick if the reader reopens it. A `choose` group is one of the page's standing asks until a pick rests on it (see $awaits): the banner counts it and `n`/`p` step the reader to it, and `settled` retires the ask with the decision.

lf-option.description: One alternative in a decision, in either of the group's two forms: lead with a <strong> title and the option is a full-width card on a row of its own, whose case can be a sentence of prose or real block content — paragraphs, valence-tagged bullets ('Good, because …'), a `<dl class="facts">` straight after the title, which docks right as a rail at one fixed width so every option's scalars align down the group, and the evidence the decision turns on: a lf-shot's before/after pair, a diagram, a figure, a widget. Put that evidence in the option it decides rather than in a section beside the group — a reader who looks in one place and presses in another is comparing from memory. Size it for the card and not for the page: an image takes whatever width it is given, a mermaid diagram takes the width its nodes need and scrolls inside the card for the rest, so a diagram written for an option is a short one, and a rail docked beside it costs 10rem of the card besides. Working that evidence is never a pick: flipping a shot, opening a `<details>`, walking a nested widget's own controls all leave the question open, and the option's own words, its chips and its mark are what answer it. Or write a short label alone, which is a question row. `for` is the id of the block on the page this option is about — the section it would change, the work it names — and renders as a reference the reader can follow. The label stays written here either way; `for` points, it never supplies words. `recommended` draws the accent ring (the author's take); `chosen` the green one (the reader's pick — the choose upgrade sets it live, and the next version carries it so the page reads right without the log). Chips are `lf-chip` children written before the title — the band a scanning eye reads first. Rewriting what a picked option says needs `restated` on that option (see $restated in `page catalog`); the other options in the group are free to change.

lf-chip.description: One label in the band above an option's or a variant's title: what the decision turns on, in the words that fit it. `effort: low` and `risk: high` are worth starting from, since most decisions do turn on those two, but they are a suggestion and nothing more — `blast-radius: high`, `backward compat: no`, `cost: £240`, `migration: two tables` are the same slot, and a chip is as free in its answer as in its name: a scale of your own, a yes or a no, a quantity, a few words. Reach for the ones the options actually differ on, write them before the <strong> title (a lf-variant takes them the same way, being the same shape without the decision), and write the same ones on every option in the group, in the same order, so they read down it. They are the glance and not the comparison — two or three an eye takes in before it reads, where a `<dl class="facts">` rail is the dimensions the options are argued on at whatever length that takes. An option can carry both, and only the rail costs a card its terseness: a `<dl>` is block content, so it stacks the group into rows, and chips never do. `tone` tints one chip — the layer's own vocabulary, `$tones.names`, which `page catalog` prints — and is the author's judgement about this answer, not a property of the facet: `risk: high` is red because you say so, and the same word on another page may not be. Leave it off and the chip is neutral, which is what most of them should be; colour that lands on every chip has stopped pointing at anything. It is the same bargain `lf-metric` makes with `direction` — the theme knows the tints, the author knows which way is good.

lf-milestones.description: A timeline of milestones with status dots on a rail. Children are lf-milestone elements only.
lf-milestones.x-example: Survey the sites Map sun and squirrel routes. Build the feeders Two classic, two heated. Install and watch

lf-milestone.description: One milestone. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. `status` colors the timeline dot; `when` is a free-text schedule label; `tags` is a comma-separated list rendered as chips.

lf-roster.description:
Who is working, and where each of them stands right now. Children are lf-agent elements only. Where lf-tasks is the work and lf-milestones the schedule, a roster is the other axis a page running several workers needs: the tree says a task is active, and only the roster says which of five sessions is holding it, what that one is doing this minute, and whether anybody has heard from it since breakfast. Reach for it on a page one orchestrator publishes and several workers report to — the standing hub arrangement — and leave it off a page with one agent on it, where the banner already says everything a roster would.

It stands wider than the prose column where the window has the room (x-wide), because a roster is read across rather than down: the comparison a reader wants is one agent's line against the next, and a column narrow enough for prose puts each line's own facts on two rows and destroys it.
lf-roster.x-example: wren Holds the feeder rebuild end to end. finch Baffles are fitted and green; the branch is yours to read. junco Free — nothing assigned since the corpus snapshot.

lf-agent.description:
One worker on the roster: a session, an agent, a person. Lead with a <strong> name — the one the worker reports under — and prose follows saying what this one is for, which is the half that does not change every ten minutes. The version carries `state`, `on`, and `branch`; the live activity clause comes only from a report.

`state` is where this worker stands: working (busy on `on`), waiting (finished, and what happens next is the reader's), blocked (stuck, and the prose or its task says on what), idle (nothing assigned), done (its part of the project is over). It is rendered as a word and not as a dot, which is the one place this widget parts company with lf-task's markers: a tree is read down its own shape, where a colour lands beside a title that already says what the work is, and a roster is read across a set of near-identical rows, where the state is the whole of what distinguishes them and a legend the reader has to hold in their head is a legend they will not. `doing` is the report's finer grain — one short clause naming the thing in front of it this minute, the per-worker twin of the detail `leaf status` puts in the banner for a page's one agent. It is generated only while that report stands. `on` names the lf-task this worker holds and renders as a reference the reader can follow; `branch` is a free-text label for where its work is landing.

Both are agent-settable through one verb (x-report), which is the whole point of the widget: `leaf report <page> ag-finch state state=working doing="rebasing onto main"` moves one row and nothing else, the page paints it live as provisional news, and it stands until a version absorbs or overrules it (see $report; `overruled` is the overruling version's word). A worker that reports keeps its own row true between versions, and the orchestrator's next version writes down what happened rather than what is happening.

One verb and not one per attribute, because the row is one sentence about one worker and both fields belong to its `activity` facet. A fold holds the last standing report per facet and unit; splitting this sentence across verbs on that same facet would make them compete for one coordinate, while assigning the fields different facets would falsely claim they can stand independently. Both fields are required for the same reason a `state` moving alone would leave an hour-old clause standing under a new word. Only `state` is recorded, which is the other half of the shape: an enum a version can absorb or overrule is worth adjudicating, and a clause that was true for a minute is not — so the sentence moves whole and only the half a version can answer creates record debt. When a version answers the report, the clause leaves with it.

The row also says when the log last heard from this worker, and that line is computed rather than authored — the newest report's own timestamp, re-read on every poll, and read past what a version has absorbed, since absorbing a report answers what the row says without hearing another word from whoever said it. It is the one fact on a hub an author cannot write down: "12 min ago" is true when the version publishes and a lie for every minute after, and a page whose freshness is stated in prose is at its least trustworthy exactly when the reader has been away longest. A worker claiming `working` that has said nothing for a quarter of an hour is called out on the row, on the same rope and by the same reckoning the banner gives a page's one agent — so "gone quiet" means one thing on the page, whoever is being judged. That rope only means anything if a working worker reports at something like that cadence, which is what the skill asks of one: silence read as a fault is a contract, not an observation.

A roster row is a view and not an ask: it is deliberately not counted among the page's standing asks (see $awaits), because what a blocked worker is waiting on is its task, and a tree already asks there. Counting both would put one interruption in front of the reader twice. What the row is instead is somewhere to point: a comment anchored on it is a message about that worker, which is how a reader says "stop, you're on the wrong file" to one of five.

lf-tasks.description: A hierarchy of work: what a project is made of, who holds each piece, and where each piece stands. Children are lf-task elements, nesting freely — the tree is the plan's own shape, so write the decomposition as it is rather than flattening it. Where lf-milestones is a flat rail of stages on a schedule and lf-board is a set the reviewer re-orders, lf-tasks is structure: a parent's children are what doing it means, and the upgrade counts each parent's subtree into a generated done-fraction chip so the tree reads as progress without a widget of its own. Statuses change by republishing, or between versions by a worker's `leaf report` (x-report on lf-task) — the page keeps up with the work — and comments anchor per task, so keep every task's id stable across versions.
lf-tasks.x-example: Rebuild the feeders Two of four mounted. Replace the mounts Fit squirrel baffles Heat the bird bath Waiting on the transformer pick below.

lf-task.description: One piece of the work. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows, and child lf-task elements after the prose are its decomposition. `status` colors the marker: planned, active, blocked (stuck — the prose says on what), review (finished by whoever held it, awaiting the reader), done. `owner` names who holds it now — an agent, a session, a person — and `when` is a free-text schedule label; both render as chips after the title, with `tags` adding one chip per entry. A parent with children also gets a generated done-fraction chip counting its subtree. A task that needs the reader's word is `review` or `blocked`: those two are the standing asks a tree makes (see $awaits), counted in the banner and stepped to by `n`/`p` alongside every other thing the page is waiting on, so keep them honest — a task marked active that is really waiting on a decision is invisible exactly where it needs to be seen. They ask until a later version says otherwise: a tree has no reader action channel, so the reader answers in words and you answer by republishing the status. The agent side does have one — `status` is agent-settable (x-report): a worker holding a task reports where it stands (`leaf report <page> <task-id> status status=review`), the page paints it as provisional news, and it stands until a version absorbs or overrules it (see $report; `overruled` is the overruling version's word).

lf-timeline.description: A chronological event log — the incident-report shape. Children are lf-event elements only. Where lf-milestones tracks planned work by status, lf-timeline records what happened, when.
lf-timeline.x-example: Feeder camera offline Battery alert from the north feeder. Battery swapped Camera back Feed resumed.

lf-event.description: One event on a timeline. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. `at` is a free-text time label; `kind` colors the dot.

lf-compare.description: Labeled variants — neutral exhibition, where lf-options is a decision. Children are lf-variant elements only. Layout follows lf-options: terse variants sit side by side, block content in any variant stacks the group into rows, and a `<dl class="facts">` after the label docks as an aligned rail.
lf-compare.x-example: Cedar Weathers silver; no sealant. Pine Cheaper; seal it yearly.

lf-variant.description: One variant in a comparison. Lead with a <strong> label; any content follows, widgets included.

lf-metrics.description: A KPI row. Children are lf-metric elements only.
lf-metrics.x-example:
<lf-metrics>
  <lf-metric id="k-visits" value="312" delta="+41" direction="up-good">daily visits</lf-metric>
  <lf-metric id="k-refills" value="2.1/wk" delta="+0.4" direction="up-bad">refills</lf-metric>
  <lf-metric id="k-species" value="14">species seen</lf-metric>
</lf-metrics>

lf-metric.description: One metric: element text is the label, `value` the headline number, `delta` a signed change (leading + or -), `direction` says which sign is good (up-good, up-bad) so the delta colors honestly; without it the delta stays neutral.

lf-diff.description: A unified diff rendered with per-file collapse, add/del tints, per-file +/− counts, and the words that moved marked on a deletion paired with the addition answering it. The body is data: the diff verbatim inside its <pre>, at column 0 (context lines keep their leading space), HTML-escaped — & as &amp; first, then < and > as &lt; and &gt;, or a diff whose lines carry entity text (&amp; in source, say) is silently altered before rendering. Comments anchor to the required id. Takes no language: each file's own path is read for one ($languages), so keep the `diff --git` or ---/+++ headers rather than pasting bare hunks, and a path naming no language leaves that file plain.
lf-diff.x-example:
diff --git a/feeders/mount.py b/feeders/mount.py
--- a/feeders/mount.py
+++ b/feeders/mount.py
@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
 def bracket():
-    return "plastic"
+    return "steel"

lf-tree.description: A file tree from an indent-notation body: one node per line, children indented deeper, a trailing / marking a directory, trailing +N/-N tokens rendering as change badges. Body is data — text inside its <pre>, HTML-escaped (& first, then < and >).
lf-tree.x-example:
feeders/
  mount.py  +2 -2
  schedule.py  +1
  sites/
    north.toml

lf-code.description: An annotated code block — the walkthrough shape. The body is the code verbatim inside its <pre> (data, HTML-escaped — & first, then < and > — column 0); `language` colors it, naming one of $languages; `hi` highlights line ranges ("3-5,8"); lf-note children sit beside that <pre> and anchor remarks at lines by number. Leave `language` off where the body isn't source (a transcript, command output) — nothing guesses, so an undeclared block stays plain.
lf-code.x-example:
def bracket(temp):
    if temp < 0:
        return "steel"
    return "cedar"
Freezing is the only threshold that matters.

lf-note.description: A remark anchored at a line of its lf-code parent. Prose content; `at` is the 1-based line number.

lf-diagram.description: A diagram rendered from a mermaid-source body (flowchart, sequence, state…). The body is data, not prose: text inside its <pre>, HTML-escaped (& first, then the angle brackets). Comments anchor to the required id, not to text inside the SVG.
lf-diagram.x-example:
graph LR
  Cart --> Pay
  Pay --> Receipt

lf-shot.description: A before/after pair of screenshots of one view, shown one at a time in a single frame: the reader clicks the image itself to swap the two, and the change is the only thing on screen that moves. The frame is the target rather than a control beside it, so the pointer rests on the change and alternates without re-aiming — which is the whole of what a flip is worth, and what a switch under the image spends. A switch sits there anyway for the keyboard, and the caption in the corner says which state is up. `before` and `after` are served image paths — `leaf page media <page> <file>…` copies files into the page directory and prints the path to write, which is the only way an image gets onto a page (a screenshot is far too many bytes to inline). `alt` says what the pair shows, for a reader who can't see it. The element takes no content: what the page has to say about the change is ordinary prose written around it, where the user can quote it. Where the change is what a decision turns on, the pair goes inside the lf-option proposing it, so the reader flips it and presses in one place. Reach for it when the change reads at page scale — layout, spacing, a component swapped out. Below that scale the column's width is against you: crop the pair to the part that moved, or show the element itself before and after at real size.
lf-shot.x-example:
The option cards

The chips now sit above the title, so a scanning eye reads cost before prose.

lf-board.description: A kanban board the user edits directly: cards move between columns or reorder within one — dragged by the grip, or by keyboard (the grip is a button: Enter grabs, arrows move, Enter drops) — and each completed move reaches the agent as a `move` action naming the card, target column, and position. Children are lf-column elements only. Write the board as you mean it and leave it alone afterwards: a recorded move carries onto every later version by itself, so re-emitting a card where you first put it does not undo the user's move. Replay preserves the exact position, but the pending mark, version diff, and restatement gate compare a card's column only: a reorder within one column is deliberately not called out as a separate state change, because raw indexes do not compose when neighbouring cards move. A move rests on its card, so revising one they have moved is the card's `restated` (see $restated in `page catalog`), never the board's.
lf-board.x-example: Heated perch Wire the south feeder. Squirrel baffle Camera mount

lf-column.description: One column on a board. `label` is the column heading, and the name a screen reader announces for the list of cards beneath it — so it has to read as the column's name on its own. Children are lf-card elements only; an empty column is a valid drop target.

lf-card.description: One card on a board. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. The user drags it by its grip; the id names it in `move` actions and keeps comment anchors stable across moves. Rewriting a card the user has moved needs `restated` on the card (see $restated in `page catalog`), which retracts the moves of that card alone — the rest of the board keeps its arrangement.

lf-tabs.description: Workstreams on one page: use one family when broad context branches into focused work. Keep the shared title and lede before it, put the current stream first, and keep earlier context intact in a sibling panel so its stable ids retain their comments and decisions. Ordering gives the first panel emphasis and makes it the default for a reader with no remembered panel or reading position. A saved panel or restored position takes precedence because the open tab is the reader's view state — remembered per browser tab like scroll position, never an action, never carried by a version. Each lf-tab is a self-contained sub-context with its own prose and widgets, while Comments, Asks, versions, and sign-off remain global. Find-in-page, ask travel, and comment-anchor jumps open the owning tab. Children are lf-tab elements only; unupgraded, panels stack as labeled sections.
lf-tabs.x-example:
Wire the first site this week.

Keep the original outcome and constraints in reach.

lf-tab.description: One workstream panel. `label` names its tab in the strip (and the stacked heading before upgrade); content is open — prose, sections, and other widgets nest freely. Ids inside share the page's one universe, so keep them distinct across tabs.

lf-draft.description: A block of text the user owns: they double-click it (or its ✎ button) to rewrite it in place, and the exact words reach the agent as an `edit` action naming the element. After the first edit, Changes shows a bounded, lossless word-aligned difference from this version, every recorded body in order, and a Restore control for each older body; very large divergent middles appear as one replacement rather than freezing the page. Restoring posts another ordinary `edit`, so it converges across tabs and later versions instead of creating private undo state. The body is the draft text verbatim inside its <pre> (data, HTML-escaped — & first, then < and >; newlines preserved). It carries no decision chrome of its own — put a draft inside a lf-card where the column is the verdict, or let page sign-off approve the page as a whole. Usable anywhere prose flows. The agent rewriting prose of its own goes in a lf-suggestion instead; a draft is the user's own words, so there is nothing for them to accept. Once they have edited one those words are theirs: re-emit the body you wrote and their edit still stands over it — and `leaf comment` reads it their way, quoting the words their edit left and refusing the ones it replaced. To take the pen back — a fact of yours to fix in a sentence they rewrote — write the new text and mark the element `restated` (see $restated in `page catalog`).
lf-draft.x-example: Adds --dry-run to every mutating command.

lf-specimen.description: Quoted material: a region the page exhibits rather than speaks — a sample decision, a demo board, markup shown as an example. Renders as quotation: a muted left gutter beside the quoted region, with a small-caps "quoted" line above it (`label` extends that line — "quoted · a decision"). Content is open and renders at full fidelity, but it is a mention, not a use: interactive widgets inside are inert — a choose group takes no clicks, a board no drags, a suggestion no decision. Keep the content visibly fictional, and let the gutter do the marking: a caption explaining that the region is an example is the page narrating a widget it could just use.
lf-specimen.x-example: effort: lowPaper maps Nothing to charge. effort: medDedicated GPS Offline maps, week-long battery.
